cases.abstract: Binary coverage errors do not capture graded costs such as the fraction of tumor pixels missed. Conformal risk control calibrates expected loss to a target alpha using a corrected calibration mean that reserves the worst-case loss of one unseen observation. For exchangeable losses bounded above by B, non-increasing and right-continuous in the prediction parameter, with terminal losses at most alpha, the selected parameter guarantees expected test loss at most alpha. With independent, identically distributed nonnegative losses and zero probability of a jump at any fixed parameter, expected risk falls no more than 2B/(n+1) below the target; this bound is tight, with n the calibration size. Segmentation, multilabel classification, hierarchical classification and question answering yield mean risks near their respective targets over 1,000 random splits. Further constructions control quantiles and multiple risks, and accommodate distribution shifts with specified weighting information. The limitation is substantive: bounded non-monotone losses can yield expected test risk arbitrarily close to B despite a smaller target. Monotone upper envelopes recover control but may be conservative, making the loss's dependence on the prediction parameter central to the guarantee.
cases.methods: The calibration rule takes the infimum over parameters satisfying (n R_n(lambda) + B)/(n+1) <= alpha, where R_n is the mean of n calibration losses, B bounds each loss above, and alpha is the target. If the constraint is unattainable, it uses a terminal parameter whose losses are at most alpha. Including B makes the criterion dominate the mean loss of the calibration observations plus one test observation. The proof compares this choice with an oracle calibrated on all n+1 losses. The corrected rule selects a parameter no smaller than the oracle's, so non-increasing losses cannot give it a larger test loss. Conditional on the unordered losses, exchangeability makes the oracle's expected test loss equal the full-sample mean, which right-continuity keeps at most alpha. The guarantee therefore averages over calibration and test observations rather than conditioning on a particular calibration sample.
cases.results: At a false-negative target of 0.1, polyp segmentation with 1,000 calibration images and 781 evaluation images achieved a mean risk of 0.0987 across 1,000 random splits, with a splitwise standard deviation of 0.0114. MS COCO multilabel classification, using 4,000 calibration and 1,000 evaluation images, yielded 0.0996 with a standard deviation of 0.0052 at the same target. Both means closely track the requested loss level, consistent with expected-risk control, while the splitwise spread distinguishes that guarantee from a ceiling on every evaluation split. The smaller COCO dispersion cannot be attributed to calibration size alone because the tasks and models also differ. The theoretical counterexample establishes a decisive boundary: without monotonicity, expected risk can approach B despite a smaller requested target, even for losses confined to [0,B]. Thus, the favorable examples support calibration for their monotone losses, not the sufficiency of boundedness alone. Upper-envelope calibration restores the guarantee by controlling a dominating monotone loss, potentially at the cost of conservatism.
cases.notes: Abstract: retained expected-loss control, the tight lower bound and monotonicity failure; the correction now explains how calibration includes the unseen observation (Theorems 1-2, Propositions 1-2). Methods: the oracle comparison connects dominance of the corrected mean to exchangeability (Section 2.1). Results: task means versus alpha test calibration, while dispersion and the counterexample delimit its interpretation (Figures 1-2, Section 2.3). Splitwise dispersions are standard deviations, not confidence intervals. Verify the QA threshold direction and stated F1 definition before using implementation details.

cases.abstract: Updating a prediction model and its calibration scores does not by itself maintain nominal coverage under distribution shift. Adaptive conformal inference calibrates the quantile's miscoverage argument through feedback: an observed miss lowers that argument, requesting a wider prediction set. With initialization in [0,1] and quantile extensions permitting full or empty sets, the discrepancy between average empirical miscoverage over T predictions and the target is bounded at order 1/(gamma T), where gamma is the update step size, regardless of the data-generating distribution. This controls long-run frequency, not coverage at every time. Under stationary hidden Markov assumptions, fixed scores and quantiles, and additional regularity, concentration and average squared marginal-error bounds relate performance to state persistence, calibration bias and optimal-parameter drift. Stock-volatility illustrations and county-vote predictions with constructed east-to-west ordering show local coverage nearer the 90% target than fixed-parameter calibration. Unnormalized volatility residuals, however, produce larger local coverage swings even with adaptation. The results distinguish correcting accumulated errors from stabilizing local coverage: faster updates improve responsiveness but increase parameter volatility, while score distributions that remain comparatively stable are also consequential.
cases.methods: At each time, adaptive conformal inference evaluates the score quantile at 1 - alpha_t using the current miscoverage parameter. Once the response arrives, the miss indicator err_t drives alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma(alpha - err_t), for target alpha and step size gamma. A miss lowers the next parameter and requests a larger set, providing corrective feedback without estimating the distribution shift. Starting from alpha_1 in [0,1], non-decreasing quantiles extended to produce full or empty sets keep the parameter in [-gamma, 1+gamma]. Summing the updates yields average(err_t) - alpha = (alpha_1 - alpha_{T+1})/(gamma T). The bounded parameter trajectory therefore controls accumulated miscoverage pathwise, rather than certifying individual predictions. The separate squared marginal-error bound requires stationary hidden Markov initialization, fixed score and quantile functions, Lipschitz statewise miscoverage and an interior parameter attaining the target in each state.
cases.results: The volatility comparison tests whether adaptive calibration helps beyond refitting the forecasting model. Both methods refit GARCH using the previous 1,250 trading days; only adaptive conformal inference updates the quantile's miscoverage argument. With normalized absolute residual scores and gamma = 0.005, adaptive coverage in centered 500-day windows stays near 90%, with fluctuations comparable to the plotted Bernoulli reference. Fixed-parameter calibration has larger departures, notably undercoverage for Fannie Mae around the 2008 crisis. The four displayed stocks were selected from twelve because fixed calibration visibly failed, so these panels illustrate difficult cases rather than estimate an average advantage. Replacing normalized scores with unnormalized residuals produces much wider local coverage swings even under adaptation. A larger step size can partly mitigate this failure, but increases parameter volatility. Thus, the normalized-score comparison supports improved local coverage in the displayed cases, while the score-change experiment shows why cumulative frequency control alone does not establish stable local coverage.
cases.notes: Abstract and Methods separate the telescoping, distribution-free frequency result (Lemma 4.1, Proposition 4.1) from the stationary hidden Markov concentration and marginal-error bounds (Theorems 4.1-4.2). Results use Figures 1-2 to test whether adaptive calibration improves local coverage beyond model refitting and to retain the unnormalized-score failure. The stock panels select four failure cases from twelve, not a representative average comparison. Figure 3 uses constructed time-zone ordering rather than observed reporting times. Bernoulli traces are visual references, not significance tests; stable local coverage is not implied by the pathwise bound.
